Early stopping: an alternative to complexity-based regularization

Early stopping is a
regularization method that doesn't involve a calculation of complexity.
Instead, early stopping simply means ending training before the model
fully converges. For example, you end training when the loss curve
for the validation set starts to increase (slope becomes positive).

Although early stopping usually increases training loss, it can decrease
test loss.

Early stopping is a quick, but rarely optimal, form of regularization.
The resulting model is very unlikely to be as good as a model trained
thoroughly on the ideal regularization rate.

The training set doesn't adequately represent real life data (or the

A model trains on a training set, but the real test of a model's worth is how

While developing a model, your test set serves as a proxy for real-world data.

Early stopping is a
regularization method that doesn't involve a calculation of complexity.
Instead, early stopping simply means ending training before the model
fully converges. For example, you end training when the loss curve
for the validation set starts to increase (slope becomes positive).

The resulting model is very unlikely to be as good as a model trained

Learning rate and
regularization rate tend to move weights in opposite

a high regularization rate pushes weights towards zero.

Take the absolute value of the difference between the actual value and the

Linear scaling is a good choice when all of the following conditions are met:

The lower and upper bounds of your data don't change much over time.

The feature contains few or no outliers, and those outliers aren't
extreme.

The feature is approximately uniformly distributed across its range.
That is, a histogram would show roughly even bars for most values.

Suppose human age is a feature. Linear scaling is a good normalization
technique for age because:

The approximate lower and upper bounds are 0 to 100.

age contains a relatively small percentage of outliers. Only about 0.3% of
the population is over 100.

Although certain ages are somewhat better represented than others, a large
dataset should contain sufficient examples of all ages.

Note: Most real-world features do not meet all of the criteria for linear
scaling. Z-score scaling is typically a better normalization choice than
linear scaling.

Quality and reliability of data

Everyone prefers high quality to low quality, but quality is such a vague
concept that it could be defined many different ways. This course defines
quality pragmatically:

A high-quality dataset helps your model accomplish its goal.
A low quality dataset inhibits your model from accomplishing its goal.

A high-quality dataset is usually also reliable.
Reliability refers to the degree to which you can trust your data.
A model trained on a reliable dataset is more likely to yield useful

In statistics and machine learning, loss measures the difference between the

the distance between the values is 3. Thus, all methods for calculating loss
remove the sign.

Take the absolute value of the difference between the actual value and the
prediction.

Square the difference between the actual value and the prediction.

quality pragmatically:

A high-quality dataset helps your model accomplish its goal.
A low quality dataset inhibits your model from accomplishing its goal.

predictions than a model trained on unreliable data.

Early stopping is a
regularization method that doesn't involve a calculation of complexity.
Instead, early stopping simply means ending training before the model
fully converges. For example, you end training when the loss curve
for the validation set starts to increase (slope becomes positive).

Although early stopping usually increases training loss, it can decrease
test loss.

Early stopping is a quick, but rarely optimal, form of regularization.
The resulting model is very unlikely to be as good as a model trained
thoroughly on the ideal regularization rate.
